what: Every departure from corpus/intmul/preregistration.json and from the plan it was written from, and every sentence of the two intake records that says more or less than the facts. Written on 2026-11-18, after the runs. Nothing in the pre-registration or in the two specs was changed; this file is read beside them. All times are UTC. Memory is in GiB (the guards' own lines print GB for the same numbers).

amendments.about: Q1, Q4 · the sentence about the planted statements (Google/CMU)
amendments.preregistered: CERTIFIED: "among the planted statements that reached the check every prediction is met".
amendments.text: Not met as written. Five of the fifteen statements planted against the Google/CMU proof (C1 and C2, the exponent 45 and 47; C5, plain n log n; C11, the time at L + 1; C6, another spelling of the logarithm) were elaborated, reached the check, and got no verdict: the check ran into the elaborator's recursion limit while unfolding the 2^46 power. Four of the five carried a prediction (refused). The record's note that they "never reached the identity check" is false for these five; the string is the tool's and is not changed here, because changing it re-derives seven older records. The sentence is read from now on as "among the planted statements that got a verdict": ten got one, each as predicted. Every statement that changes the saving is among the five, so as run the intake's check did not show that it tells κ = 2^-46 from κ = 2^-45. Two checks were added after the run to show it: (a) a structural comparison of every planted statement of both specs with its statement, as expressions and with nothing unfolded (corpus/intmul/checks/first, results in corpus/intmul/pod/extra/struct): every changed statement differs; (b) comparator on the release's own nine controls, where the exponent-45 control is refused because the statement does not match. The word for the Google/CMU proof stays CERTIFIED with this amendment named beside it.

amendments.about: Q1 · what the Google/CMU intake record says about kernels, identity and hypotheses
amendments.text: "kernels: ACCEPT (3 run)" counts three entries; they are two kernels, and the second entry (leanchecker without --fresh) replayed a module of two declarations. In the registered run Lean's kernel checked the release's modules as they were built from source (Mathlib's compiled files came from its cache), and nanoda checked the whole closure, Mathlib included (124,416 declarations). A fresh replay of the whole closure by Lean's kernel (leanchecker --fresh on the headline module) was run afterwards and exits 0. In this spec the statement is given as a named definition, so F1's "equal as expressions" compares that name with itself and could not come out false; the evidence that the name is the text of the pinned file is the planted statement S0 (the body typed out, accepted) and the file's sha256. F3's CERTIFIED cannot fail in this mode and reports nothing; the statement was read by hand to be a bare existence claim with no hypothesis. The controls summary line "3 refused, 0 accepted, of 3 (kernel decides)" misdescribes this spec. The record's hazards scan covers the 25-line theorem file only, and its two hits are comments; a scan of every Lean file of both releases is in corpus/intmul/checks/first/hazards.json (a flag, never a verdict).

amendments.about: Q4 · a count in the pre-registration
amendments.text: Three do: C6 and C9 of the Google/CMU spec, C8 of the community spec.

amendments.about: Q1 · the community proof's second kernel, and how the registered run ended
amendments.text: The registered run did not end by itself. 76 minutes into its nanoda step (03:35:38) the run's own memory watchdog stopped it at 114,017 MiB of the container's 122,070 (it counts file cache); the run's exit is 143. At that moment the pod was shared: nanoda on the joined theorem's export had been running since 02:25, and a tool for the optional checks (con-leche) was being built from 03:12:53 to 03:36:04, by us. The container's memory rose from about 69,000 MiB to 114,017 MiB over exactly that interval. How much of the rise was nanoda's own and how much was ours cannot be separated from the log. The step was run again by hand from the same binary, configuration and export (sha256 of each in _resumed.json), started 03:40:07. It held under 9 GiB for about 70 minutes, then grew past 100 GiB in the next ten, and our guard stopped it at 05:01:01 with nanoda alone at 114.8 GiB (exit 137, 4,868.8 s). The record's word for that kernel, "REJECTS OR STOPPED", is the tool's; it was stopped both times and never printed a rejection. The verdict for the community proof is REFUSED on resources. No larger machine was rented: the plan says to ask first.

amendments.about: Q1, Q3 · the same growth in four runs and three checkers, cause not found
amendments.text: Memory grew past 100 GiB after a long flat stretch in four runs whose input contains the community proof: nanoda on the registered export (A4); nanoda on the joined theorem's export (started 02:25; the first reading of it alone is 48.4 GiB at 04:09:51 and the last 103.5 GiB at 04:14:11; stopped by our guard at 04:14:26); and Lean's own kernel replaying the whole closure afresh (leanchecker --fresh on the theorem's module: started 03:36; under 12 GiB in every reading from 04:09 to 09:54, then to 115.2 GiB in under half an hour, stopped by hand at 10:18:25 after 24,104 s, no output); and con-leche on the registered export (A8), the one run of the four made on an otherwise empty pod. Three checkers written independently show it. During the normal build Lean's kernel accepted every module of the same proof inside the same memory. The cause was not found. One guess was tested and not supported: a scan of both exports for very large number literals (corpus/intmul/checks/diag/big_literals.py) found none near the size of an exponent; the largest are certificate data of up to 52,939 bits. Nothing was sent to the authors of either tool.

amendments.planned: comparator with nanoda against our own copy of each statement, typed from the paper.
amendments.text: Run after the registered runs, and not against a statement typed from the paper. Google/CMU: the release's own challenge module and configurations (one positive, nine controls), in a copy of the checkout with the release's own lakefile addition appended and replay/Replay copied to ./Replay; comparator v4.33.0 (3927ad38) built on Lean 4.33.1 with lean4export 15f6055e. The first attempt ended in a stack overflow inside nanoda, with the intake's nanoda build 8de7e0c4 (comparator writes nanoda's configuration with no stack size); the run that counts used the nanoda commit the release names (37cb87b7). It accepts under both kernels, and the nine controls come out as the release's replay record says. So this is a second party repeating the authors' own check on another machine, not a new kind of check. Community: the release ships no challenge module; one was written here (corpus/intmul/checks/xreplay) and installed in the registered checkout after the registered run was over, with comparator v4.34.0 (d03acab1) on Lean 4.34.1, lean4export 076e8e57, nanoda switched off because of A4. The control (the saving's numerator raised by one) is refused: the statement does not match. The run on the true statement gave no verdict: our guard stopped it after 5 h 14 min when the fresh replay beside it passed 100 GiB; it held 7.4 GiB and had printed nothing after its build. It was not run again. The sandbox: landrun v0.1.18 (ec104f6e) through comparator's own --best-effort on a kernel whose Landlock ABI is 4; the pod has no systemd, so the README's RestrictAddressFamilies property was not applied and the stack limit was set with ulimit.

One try each, as optional checks. No lean4lean commit names Lean 4.33.1 or 4.34.1; its master (67f63b0c, on 4.33.0-rc2) was built with each toolchain forced. On 4.33.1 it builds: the headline module alone exits 0 ("checked 1 declarations", which is one declaration and says little); the fresh replay of the closure stopped after 30 min 45 s at "(kernel) deep recursion detected" in SubNLogN.Machine.C5.NetAux.pm_hdMinus. That is lean4lean reaching its own limit, not a rejection, and it gives no verdict. On 4.34.1 it does not build (Batteries.Data.List.Basic fails), so it was not run on the community proof.

con-leche master (cd2eceab, its own toolchain Lean 4.36.0) was run on each registered export in its default mode (--verified), with 8 threads, as the last optional check. Google/CMU: "accepted 120324 declarations", exit 0, 2 min 33 s. Its count is not nanoda's 124,416 on the same file; the two tools count differently and the difference was not reconciled. Community: no verdict. From 10:22, when the other con-leche run ended, it was alone on the pod: every reading for 53 minutes was under 10 GiB, and all but the first under 5; then it grew by about 17 GiB a minute, and our guard stopped it at 11:22:17 at 100.7 GiB, 62 min 48 s after its start; no output. con-leche is a third checker, not the pre-registered second kernel; its acceptance of the Google/CMU proof is stated beside that verdict and does not change the word.

amendments.about: Q3, plan P5 · the theorem joining the two statements
amendments.planned: 5a the two forms of the bound; 5b a transducer between the two input encodings, one day at most, a written argument if it does not close.
amendments.text: Both closed, and more was built than planned: one theorem, IntMulBridge.community_proves_challenge, whose type is the Google/CMU statement, compiled in the community release's environment with the community theorem imported and the Google/CMU statement file copied byte for byte. To get the finite-alphabets clause, which the community statement does not have, IntMulBridge/Finite.lean rebuilds the community machine along the community's own chain of lemmas; it is not proved equal to the machine inside their existential theorem. The other direction is not built. Lean's kernel only: nanoda on the export was stopped on memory (A5). corpus/intmul/bridge/assembly/check.log was written on a text of Encodings.lean that differs from the final one in one comment line (corpus/intmul/pod/extra/bridge-encodings-comment.diff); all five modules were compiled again from the final texts before the export, and their sha256 on the pod equal the files kept here. The exporter for the joined theorem was lean4export at cacf989 (the bump to v4.34.0-rc2), and nanoda was configured to treat an unpermitted axiom as a hard error.

amendments.about: stop rule · "If the google-cmu run does not reproduce what its authors report, the community run is stopped until the difference is read."
amendments.text: The authors report their exponent-45 control refused by comparator. Our intake's exponent controls got no verdict, by another method (A1). The rule was read as not triggered, because no check contradicted the authors and the record came out as expected, and the community run started at 00:15 without a stop. A stricter reading would have stopped it. The comparator run made later reproduces all nine of their controls.

The pre-registration and the two specs were committed at 2026-11-17 23:15:04, 47 seconds before the pod was created (23:15:51), on a local branch that was not pushed. Their digest reached a public place only at 2026-11-18 01:09:48 (the seal registry of this repository, commit 14b9f72a): after the first result (the Google/CMU record, 00:04) and before the second. The public clock therefore proves the pre-registration existed before the community result and before every optional check, not before the Google/CMU result.

amendments.about: tool versions the records do not name
amendments.text: For Lean 4.33.1 the intake tool picked lean4export by sorting tags and took 9fb131b ("bump toolchain to v4.33.0-rc2"), then set its toolchain to 4.33.1. The export it wrote was accepted by nanoda and by con-leche. The nanoda configuration of the registered Google/CMU run was written to the work folder, not to the facts; a copy is in corpus/intmul/pod/extra/gcmu-nanoda.json. No planted defect reaches the second kernel in the registered runs (they are caught by the list of axioms in a Lean build); afterwards one, the added axiom, was exported and shown to nanoda, which fails on it in both of its modes (corpus/intmul/pod/extra/red-R2-*).

amendments.about: Q2 · "the encodings evaluated on small pairs against an encoder of our own"
amendments.text: Done after the first result, not before: 328 pairs for each release, produced by an encoder written here and evaluated in Lean against each release's encoder; every one holds. The two readings were made before the runs, by readers who did not see each other's notes, and both worked their examples by hand.

The Python reference's own test suite was not run. The first pass of the Python rows (216, all exact) carried labels that said more than ran and recorded no counter; a second pass (236 rows, all exact) records the library's own counters for each row and replaces the first for every statement about which path ran. Zero and one, and 10^8 bits in the program's other mode, were added to the C rows in the second pass. The first C script would read an empty product file as zero; no row depends on it. Sizes above 10^8 bits were not run.
Every time in these files was taken on a pod that was doing something else at the same moment. None is a speed, and none is quoted as one.

amendments.about: said during the run and corrected
amendments.text: Three statements made while the pod was running were wrong and were corrected the same day: that three kernels had accepted the Google/CMU proof (at the time one of the three had replayed a two-declaration module; the fresh replay came later); that the Python reference had run "under schedules that force the new route" (the counters show what ran); and that the first stop of the community run was caused by our tool build alone (A4: it cannot be separated).
